en: The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-pravāraṇā-karma*,
one fascicle;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, for the three-month rains retreat.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who were observing the rains retreat in other locations; they had each established a regulation, saying:
"Venerable friends!..."
During our three-month *varṣā* retreat, we should not speak of those who have broken their precepts, their views, or their rules of conduct, nor of those with improper livelihoods.
If one sees that the toilet grass is depleted or that the water jar is empty, one should immediately replenish them and restore them to their original places.
"If you are unable to do it alone, you should call a companion with your hand and work together.
Having established this rule, they each returned to their former places and remained thus without speaking.

When the three months were completed, having finished mending and washing their robes, they donned their garments and took up their bowls, gradually traveling from their place of retreat toward the city of Śrāvastī.
Having arrived, each placed away his robes and bowl; after washing his feet, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they first offer him consolation and inquiry:
"From where have you come?"
"Is the road safe and pleasant?
Where do you dwell? He replied:

"We have completed the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) at Caṇḍaprabha; we have just returned from there. During that retreat, we lived in great peace and harmony, and we did not find even alms-seeking to be a hardship."

However, we many bhikṣus, during those three months of the rainy season retreat, each established a regulation that we would not speak to one another throughout the retreat; as fully described in the aforementioned rules for establishing such regulations, we dwelt in peace and happiness, without being troubled by the need to beg for alms.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You are all foolish; there is not a single person among you who possesses wisdom.
How can you establish such an illegal regulation as to forbid one another from speaking?"
It is just like dwelling with an enemy and eating an enemy’s food; this is truly suffering.
How can you say that one dwells in peace and happiness?
This is the teaching of outsiders, a teaching of ignorance, not a teaching of the essential way out.
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, from this day forward, those who practice the method of silent muteness shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
When the bhikṣus have completed the rains retreat, the Buddha said:
"One should request the three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected—to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
Once the bhikṣus were instructed to perform the ceremony regarding these three matters of what was seen, heard, and suspected, they did not know how to proceed.
The Buddha said:

"Seven or eight days before the departure, all resident bhikṣus should go to the nearby villages and inform all the bhikṣus, both old and young, as well as those who have not yet received full ordination, that they should all together prepare for the offerings. On the fourteenth day of the eighth month, they must perform various offerings at the Buddha hall and the vicinity of the caitya:
burning incense, hanging banners, and arranging all manner of decorations—all of these should be carried out."

If the upādhyāya, the ācārya, and all their disciples are made to prepare everything together—including sweeping and sprinkling, smearing the ground with cow dung, and providing the Saṃgha with offerings such as excellent food and drink, along with clarified butter and other articles of worship—these should be arranged according to the occasion.
The bhikṣus should comfort one another, saying:
"Our summer retreat has been very peaceful and pleasant.
On the fourteenth night, they should have those who uphold the sūtras recite them throughout the entire night.
Tomorrow, when you recognize the proper time, perform the *sāṃghika-pravāraṇā* ceremony; do not let it pass until the appearance of dawn.

When the next day arrives, one should appoint those possessing the five virtues to perform the *pravāraṇā* for the community—whether it be one, two, or many individuals—but they must be persons endowed with these five virtues.
If those who were previously discordant can be brought into harmony, and those already in harmony are made to dwell in supreme happiness—what are these five? They are:
being without attachment, without aversion, without fear, without delusion, and being skillfully able to distinguish matters such as one's own wishes as they arise.
If these five qualities are reversed, one should not be appointed.
Since he possesses these five virtues, he should be appointed in this manner:
having prepared the seats and mats, struck the *ghanṭā*, assembled the *saṃgha*, and performed the preliminary rites, and having asked the assembly for their consent, he should exhort them:
"O [Name], are you able to perform the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha of the summer retreat by means of the three matters— what has been seen,
heard, or suspected? He replies,
"I am able."
Next, one bhikṣu should first make a formal announcement (jñapti) before performing the ritual act (karman):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so, shall now serve as the bhikṣu for the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā) for the Saṃgha observing the summer retreat."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha authorize that the Saṃgha now appoint such-and-such a person as the *pravāraṇā* bhikṣu; this such-and-such person shall serve as the *pravāraṇā* bhikṣu for the Saṃgha that has completed the summer retreat.
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, now acts as the bhikṣu for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on behalf of the Saṃgha observing the summer retreat."
The Saṃgha now appoints so-and-so as the *pravāraṇā* bhikṣu; so-and-so shall act as the *pravāraṇā* bhikṣu for the Saṃgha that has completed the summer retreat.

If the venerable ones consent to so-and-so being appointed as the *pravāraṇā* bhikṣu, and agree that so-and-so shall act as the *pravāraṇā* bhikṣu for the Saṃgha that has completed the summer retreat, let them remain silent;
if you do not consent, please speak.
"The Saṃgha has already authorized so-and-so to act as the *pravāraṇā* monk for the summer retreat Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by its silence; thus do I now uphold this decision."
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus! I shall now establish the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu performing the Pravāraṇā ceremony."
Listen attentively!
I shall now speak.
A bhikṣu who has received the invitation to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony should provide fresh *kuśa* grass to serve as a seat for the bhikṣus.
If there is only one person acting as the recipient of the *pravāraṇā*, he should receive the *pravāraṇā* from the senior monk (*sthavira*) and proceed down through the ranks to the junior-most monk.
If there are two persons, one shall receive it from the senior monk, and the other from the middle of the assembly down to the end of the line.
If three persons are appointed, they shall arise from three locations; this may be understood according to the circumstances.
All the bhikṣus shall sit upon mats of *kuśa* grass, remaining in a squatting posture.
The senior monk (*sthavira*) should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha is performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and you grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now perform the *pravāraṇā*."
"Thus it is declared.
The bhikṣu who is to receive the *pravāraṇā* should approach the elder (*sthavira*) and remain there squatting.

At that time, the elder and the other junior monks (*navaka*) should spread fresh *kuśa* grass, laying it crosswise with the tips pointing downward; they should then draw their bodies close forward, tread upon it with both feet, bend their hands slightly, and hold them before them, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sir, please take note!
Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day; I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day."
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], before the Saṃgha and in the presence of the Venerable Ones, perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony regarding matters seen, heard, or suspected. "Venerable Saṃgha!..."
Please accept me and instruct me; please benefit and have compassion for me.
O compassionate one, out of your compassion, if you perceive and see my transgression, I shall confess it according to the Dharma and the Vinaya.
The second and third times should also be spoken in this manner.
The bhikṣu who receives the *pravāraṇā* should say: "Aubhika."
He replied, "Sādhu. In this manner,
it was said in succession until the junior monk, who spoke likewise.
Regarding those who perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish), they should mutually perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony toward one another, and this should also be recited three times.
If there are two, three, four, or even more bhikṣus receiving the *pravāraṇā*, they should perform it in mutual relation with one another.
If there is but one person, he should perform the *pravāraṇā* in the presence of the person who has already performed his own *pravāraṇā*; the procedure for this is to be understood by analogy.

Once the bhikṣus have finished, the community of bhikṣuṇīs is next summoned; each is made to enter the assembly and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in the presence of the bhikṣu performing the *pravāraṇā*, according to the rules for the great bhikṣus.

Next, summon the śikṣamāṇās, the male śrāmaṇeras, and the female śrāmaṇerīs; each must, in their respective order, stand before a bhikṣu endowed with the five virtues and undergo the ritual procedure as previously described.
The bhikṣu who is to receive the *pravāraṇā* should stand before the elder and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable sisters! The *pravāraṇā* of both Saṃghas has been completed."
The Saṃgha of both divisions should together proclaim:
"Excellent! The *pravāraṇā* has been performed; it has been very well performed.
It is good if they so proclaim; if they do not proclaim this, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).

The bhikṣu who is to receive the invitation (pravāraṇā) should carry a small knife, or a needle and thread, or various other requisites of a śramaṇa, stand before the elder (sthavira), and speak as follows:
"Venerable One!..."
May these various items be offered as a *pravāraṇā* gift to those who have completed their *varṣā* retreat?
Furthermore, if other items for the benefit of the community are acquired at this location, should the harmonious *saṃgha* divide them?
The entire assembly answered simultaneously, saying,
"It should be divided.
If it were otherwise, both the *svacchanda* bhikṣu and the rest of the great assembly would all incur an offense against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how many kinds of *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) are there?"
The Buddha said: "There are four kinds:
first, an illegal assembly that is divided;..."
2. Illegitimate concord; 3. Legitimate discord; 4. Legitimate concord.
The Buddha said:
"Upāli! Among these four, that which is in accordance with the Dharma and performed in harmony is the virtuous one."
Because the Dharma was thus harmonized, on the fifteenth day during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony,
the Blessed One took his seat within the Saṃgha.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"The night has passed; why do you not go as you please?
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat amidst the assembly, adjusted his robe to one shoulder, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed them, saying:
"In such-and-such a room there is a resident bhikṣu who is afflicted with a grave illness and is suffering greatly."
"The sick bhikṣu is unable to attend the assembly; what should he do?
The Buddha said, "He should come bringing his consent for the *pravāraṇā*."
The bhikṣus did not know how to take the *chanda* (consent) and bring it back.
The Buddha said:
"Either one person may take the *chanda* of one person, or two, or three, or even many."
Not knowing how to bring it back, the Buddha said:

"One should go to the side of the sick bhikṣu, squat down with palms joined and having established proper deportment; then, according to the procedure for the Poṣadha, one should grant him the consent (chanda), speaking as follows:"
"Venerable sir, please take note!
Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], declare that I am free from all obstructing conditions;
however, due to the cause and condition of illness, I now grant my consent (*chanda*) for that legal matter of the Saṃgha. You should explain this matter to me as it is presented.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.
If one can grant the *chanda* (consent) in this way, it is well;
if one is unable to speak, it is still accomplished as granting the *chanda* by means of bodily indicative action (*kāyavijñapti*).
If the patient is unable to speak and also unable to express themselves through physical gestures, the entire Saṃgha should go together to the patient's location.
If the patient does not come and the assembly does not go there to perform the *pravāraṇā*, the ritual act is not accomplished, and one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmāpatti*).
The Buddha said:
"I shall now explain the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu who receives the *chanda* (consent) for the *pravāraṇā*.
That bhikṣu receiving the consent must not run quickly, and so forth, as explained in detail in the section on the *poṣadha* ceremony."
Once that bhikṣu who holds the desire for purity has entered the assembly, he may announce it to the side of the elder (sthavira).
If he is unable to do so, it is also permissible to announce it to a neighboring seat. He should speak thus:
"Venerable one, please attend! [The rest as before]."
In a certain room, the bhikṣu named [Name], is afflicted by the suffering of illness.
Now, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha shall perform the *pravāraṇā*; that bhikṣu named [Name] shall likewise perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day.

That bhikṣu, so-and-so, has personally declared that he is free from all obstructing conditions; for the sake of his illness, he has granted his consent (*chanda*) for the legal business of the Saṃgha.
I now fully relate what he has declared.
"As has been stated above, if one does not comply, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying, "Bhadanta!..."
"If, after having received the *chanda* (consent) for the *pravāraṇā*, one should suddenly die on the way, would this constitute a valid holding of the consent?
The Buddha said:
"It does not constitute [a valid holding]; one should receive the consent again."
This is explained in detail, exactly as in the *Poṣadha* [Karmavācanā].
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bhadanta!..."
"If there is a residence where only a single bhikṣu dwells alone, how should he perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony?
The Buddha said:

"He should sprinkle water to sweep and clean the residence, smear it with cow dung, and arrange the seats and mats. Having completed these communal tasks, he should recite a small or large portion of the Sūtras according to his capacity. Then, from a high and distant place, he should look in all four directions to see if any other bhikṣus are coming, thereby knowing whether the assembly is pure."
If there are two or three people, they should immediately call out to one another to come quickly and together perform the *svairakāra* (the rite of acting according to one's own will).
Then, in the presence of those visiting bhikṣus, they should perform the ritual of face-to-face address (*pratyekamukha-dharma*) by speaking as follows:
"Venerable one, please attend!..."
Today, the fifteenth day, is the day for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall likewise observe the *pravāraṇā* for this fifteenth day.
At a later time, when I encounter a harmonious assembly, I shall perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma together with that harmonious assembly.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.
If there are many ignorant and deluded persons among them who suffice the required number for the *sāmagrī* (formal assembly), the *sāmagrī-karma* is not validly accomplished.
One should wait for a virtuous bhikṣu to arrive so that they may perform the *pravāraṇā* together.
If none is present, one should remain in one's original seat and perform the mental *pravāraṇā*, speaking these words of intention:
"Today is the fifteenth day, the day of *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [Name], likewise perform the mental *pravāraṇā* on this fifteenth day."
"If at a later time there is an assembly that acts according to the Dharma, they shall together perform the *pravāraṇā*.
Thus it is said three times.
If there are one, two, or three bhikṣus living together, they should likewise perform the *pravāraṇā* using the method of addressing one another (*pratyekavācanā*), as previously described.

If there are four members of the Saṃgha performing the *pravāraṇā*, they should all perform it as a face-to-face (*pratyekamukha*) ceremony; they do not appoint five virtuous persons to conduct the *pravāraṇā* rite.
If there are five or more, it constitutes a formal assembly (*saṃghakarma*), and one should then perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the *pravāraṇā* rite.
If there is a sick person who ought to enter the assembly, they should not give their consent (*chanda*).
If there are six persons, or more than that, everyone shall perform a *jñapti* (a single motion) for the sake of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
When performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, if there is a sick person, one should have them convey their consent (*chanda*).
There may be cases where one [monk] conducts the *pravāraṇā* in accordance with the Dharma while another does so contrary to the Dharma;
or three conduct it according to the Dharma while one does so contrary to the Dharma.
Five are lawful (dharma), and one is unlawful (adharma).
What is the one that is lawful in its cessation and according to the will, and what is the one that is unlawful?
If one has merely spoken once and then immediately ceases, this is called unlawful.
If explained in full, this is called "the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma.
Why are three [cases] considered according to the Dharma and one not?
When the three have completed the recitation of the *pravāraṇā* and then ceased, this is called "according to the Dharma."
Having recited it once, he then stops; this is called illegal (*adharma*).
What are the five that are legal (*dharma*) and the one that is illegal?
Among them, one [instance] is according to the Dharma (*dharmika*), which combines three recitations for the *pravāraṇā*.
If one speaks only once and then stops, this is called an illegal *prātimokṣa* (formal confession) procedure.
There may be cases where the *prātimokṣa* is accomplished by speaking once, or by speaking twice or thrice; at other times, the entire assembly speaks simultaneously.
On what basis is the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) spoken of as being performed once?

If on the fifteenth day, a large number of bhikṣus assemble in one place intending to perform the *pravāraṇā*, yet many among the assembly suffer from hemorrhoids, and if they were to recite it three times, there is concern that the sick bhikṣus would be unable to endure sitting for so long. For this reason, the Buddha said:
"One may perform the *pravāraṇā* by a single proclamation.
Furthermore, there were many bhikṣus gathered in one place for the purpose of performing the *pravāraṇā*, when it either rained or was about to rain.
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"If we recite it three times, we fear the rain will fall and dampen our bedding.
For this reason, the Buddha permitted them to perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it once.
Furthermore, there were many bhikṣus gathered in one place for the ceremony of *pravāraṇā*.
At that residence, either a king arrived with his retinue, or high ministers and their subordinates, as well as people from within and outside the city, all likewise assembled there.
He presented various foods, drinks, garments, and other requisites to the community of bhikṣus and requested them to offer prayers of blessing.
The bhikṣus spent the entire night offering these prayers, undergoing great hardship.
However, each of the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Because the king and others have come and offered various gifts, we have performed the ritual of incantation and prayer with great hardship; we fear that the dawn will break."
For this reason, he permitted the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) to be performed with a single recitation.
Furthermore, at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, when a great number of bhikṣus had gathered together intending to perform the *pravāraṇā*,
those among them who were learned in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās spent the entire night reciting the scriptures and preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus each had this thought:
"This bhikṣu who is learned in the Tripiṭaka has spent the entire night reciting sūtras and preaching the Dharma; he has undergone great hardship."
"However, fearing that dawn may break before we can recite it three times,
we shall therefore permit you to perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it once according to your wish.
Furthermore, during the time of the *pravāraṇā*, if any of the four kinds of disputes arise, one should consult a *bhikṣu* learned in the Tripiṭaka to adjudicate the offenses.
Once the offense had been removed, those bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"This bhikṣu of the Tripiṭaka has spent the entire night resolving this dispute; he has undergone extreme hardship."
Furthermore, fearing that daybreak might arrive, they recited the *pravāraṇā* three times;
however, this was feared to cause an obstruction. For this reason, it was permitted to recite the *pravāraṇā* once.
Moreover, at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, there may be kings who arrive at their dwelling place with the fourfold army—namely, elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry.
The king, filled with rage, spoke these words: "Seize this śramaṇa son of the Śākyas and bind him!

Make him attend to the elephants and the horses; I shall now employ him in various miscellaneous tasks to exhaust his strength. Or he may issue such a command: "Seize the śramaṇa, strip him of his robes and bowl, and put them all to death."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves: "If we perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it three times, we fear the King will become angry and reprimand us, leading to an unbeneficial outcome.
For this reason, they were granted permission to perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it only once.

If, during the period of *pravāraṇā*, there are bandits and the like—those who destroy cities or villages, or thieves who kill the cattle and sheep of others—or those who kill cattle and sheep and smear their blood upon the lintels, doors, and windows as part of unlawful rites, or if they send messengers to summon the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"If we perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony by reciting the formal proclamation three times, we fear those bandits will destroy the cities and villages, and slaughter the cattle and sheep."
"Since they have committed an illegal act and have come to summon me for an unbeneficial matter— whether to seize my robes and bowl or to take my life—
it is for this reason that the Noble One has opened the way for a single recitation to constitute the *pravāraṇā*."

If, during the period of *pravāraṇā*, there is in this residence an elderly bhikṣu who is ignorant by nature and suffers from excessive mucus and spittle; or one who has come from afar and is exhausted from the journey; or if there are women, or young girls, or disputes; or if there is no faith [in the Dharma], but rather in Māras, celestial demons, and various evil spirits.
Coming to the gate, they spoke these words: "Śramaṇas! You have committed impure acts;
you have spat upon the beds and mats, or suffered from upward-moving wind and downward-dropping diarrhea."
Furthermore, the various deities caused the bhikṣus to attend to the illnesses of spirits and ghosts.
The bhikṣus thought:
"If I perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony by reciting it three times, there are currently many obstacles that will cause me unrest."
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony once;

there is no offense. Suppose monks construct a monastic dwelling in a place inhabited by fierce beasts, and in that location there are elderly women, ignorant women, and young girls whose nature is not pure or clean.

However, because the bhikṣus defiled their bedding and seats by urinating and defecating in improper ways, and washed their worn-out clothes and hung them out to dry, they caused resentment among the spirits and deities. This led harmful and venomous beasts—such as tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, and bears—to come and harm the bhikṣus. These creatures would arrive at the monasteries, or in individual rooms, at the walls, at eating places, and indeed everywhere, creating obstacles in all locations.
He wished to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony three times, but fearing that obstacles might arise, the Noble One permitted it to be performed once.

If there is a bhikṣu who dwells near the abode of a nāga, he may commit various kinds of impurities—such as spitting or blowing his nose excessively, suffering from upward-moving or downward-discharging ailments, or passing excrement and urine—which constitute many forms of uncleanness. This causes the nāga to become enraged; he may release various venomous insects to harm the bhikṣu, or the nāga may come in person and say to the bhikṣu:
"In my place, you have committed many such impurities as mentioned above, which are contrary to the Dharma."
The bhikṣu thought to himself,
"If I perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting three times, I fear there may be dangers such as nāgas.
For this reason, the Noble One permitted a single recitation or a simultaneous recitation before others.

If at a time when a monastery is situated near the houses of laypeople, and a bhikṣu wishes to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, a fire suddenly breaks out in those lay dwellings; and that fire gradually approaches the monastery, or there is fear of dangers such as loss of life or the violation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or damage to robes and bowls.

If one fears that a fire is imminent when performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony three times, for this reason it is permitted to perform the *pravāraṇā* once; or, if one performs the *pravāraṇā* by addressing [the preceptor] all at once, there is no offense.

If a monastic dwelling is situated near a great mountain valley and, during the period of *pravāraṇā*, heavy rain falls from the heavens, causing the waters to swell and overflow, inundating the royal palaces, villages, forests, gardens, and trees, and gradually pressing against the monastery.

If one were to recite it three times, there might be danger to the lives of the bhikṣus or danger to their robes and bowls; for this reason, the Noble One has permitted a single recitation or a simultaneous face-to-face recitation.
If a bhikṣu’s residence is located in a remote wilderness where dangers arise and there is fear for one's life and so forth,
the bhikṣus shall inform one another, saying:
"Today, the fifteenth day, is the time for the *pravāraṇā*."

"Since we have encountered such urgent and difficult circumstances, we may not perform the *pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of mutual invitation) at our leisure or according to our own wishes; we shall instead perform the *pravāraṇā* rite in accordance with the Dharma later on.
If such circumstances as these arise, and one rises suddenly and simultaneously [to leave], there is no offense whatsoever.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are many bhikṣus who have entered the rainy season retreat together, and before the period has expired, they wish to travel to other places."
"Can one then immediately obtain it as one wishes? The Buddha said, "No."
If one says,
"I shall suspend the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for now and perform it later at another location," the bhikṣus should reply:
"Venerable ones!
We are observing the rains retreat here; we must not perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony elsewhere, nor suspend the *pravāraṇā*.
The Buddha has commanded us that once we have completed the rains retreat in accordance with the Dharma, we shall subsequently perform the *pravāraṇā* in accordance with the Dharma."
If a bhikṣu says: "I have a matter to attend to and must depart;
you should perform the *pravāraṇā* for me and postpone the *pravāraṇā*, waiting until he returns."
"Is it obtained? The Buddha said, "Upāli!"
This does not constitute a valid *pravāraṇā*. He should reply:
"It was originally improper for me to entrust you with the *pravāraṇā* or to suspend the *pravāraṇā*; I shall wait until the *varṣā* retreat is concluded."

"The Buddha has permitted us to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony after our *varṣā* retreat is complete; thereafter, we may perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma and in a state of purity. He does not permit us to perform the *pravāraṇā* in a manner that is contrary to the Dharma.
The Buddha said, "Upāli!"
As stated above, if one does not act in accordance with these instructions and performs what is contrary to the Dharma, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If, on the fifteenth day at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, a bhikṣu is suddenly seized by a king, or seized by a minister, or seized by bandits, or seized by an enemy.
The assembly of bhikṣus there should send a messenger to inform them, saying:
"Please release this bhikṣu for a short while; there is a minor matter requiring his presence.
If they release him, that is well.
If they do not release him, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* within a small boundary (*kṣudrasīman*).
Once the monk who was seized has later been released, they must perform the *pravāraṇā* again.
If they do not do so, they incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).

If a bhikṣu reaches the time for the Pravāraṇā ceremony and recalls that he has committed an offense, he must first perform the rite of confession before other bhikṣus; only then may he proceed with the Pravāraṇā.
If one performs the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony) without having confessed one's offenses, the *pravāraṇā* is not valid.
This is explained in detail within the rules for the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony), and it is also explained in detail regarding the ten matters.

If, when the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony arrives, a bhikṣu remembers and recognizes that he has committed an offense and wishes to confess it, if it is a *pārājika* offense, the community should expel him first, and only then proceed with the *pravāraṇā*.
If there is one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, that offense should be set aside for the time being;

first, having performed the *pravāraṇā*, one shall subsequently undergo disciplinary action. If the offenses are *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta*, one should first confess and repent, and only afterwards perform the *pravāraṇā*.

If a bhikṣu, when the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony arrives, conceives doubt regarding a *pārājika* offense—whether it actually constitutes a *pārājika* or not—if he has committed a *pārājika*, he shall no longer live in communion; he does not remain a bhikṣu.
If one is not subject to non-residence (asaṃvāsa) and other such conditions, one should remain for a while and then perform the *pravāraṇā*.

If, at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, there is a bhikṣu who has been charged with an offense or subjected to a formal act (*karmavācanā*), and that person has confessed their offense, they should first confess the offense and only then perform the *pravāraṇā*.
For those who have been excluded by means of a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one should first perform the ritual before subsequently conducting the *pravāraṇā*.
If, at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, some bhikṣus should say to one another,
"You have committed an offense," [the procedure must be adjusted].
If the bhikṣu who has raised the charge is not virtuous in body, speech, and mind, one should not speak to him, but should instead proceed with the *pravāraṇā*.
If, during the time of the *pravāraṇā*, there is a bhikṣu who raises a charge, one should first observe whether this person guards their body, speech, and mind.
If this person’s body is well-restrained but their speech is not, one should not employ speech; rather, one should act according to one's own inclination.
If they can well-guard their speech but their body is not well-restrained, one should likewise not employ speech.

Even if one well guards body and speech, if they are not proficient in the Tripiṭaka, they should likewise not be permitted to speak, and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) should proceed according to their preference.

At the time of the *pravāraṇā*, there may be a bhikṣu who raises a charge who, though well-guarding body and speech and having studied the Tripiṭaka, does not understand its profound meaning nor possesses clear comprehension.
One should tell him:
"Examine this thoroughly, and then remove my offense according to the Dharma. One should then perform the *cārayitavya* (the formal act of seeking absolution).

If, at the time of the *caitya-vandana* (or *svacchanda*), there are bhikṣus who well-guard their body and speech, study the Tripiṭaka, thoroughly understand its meaning, and are proficient in its practical application.

Furthermore, with a deluded mind, he went into the midst of the Saṃgha and spoke what is Dharma as non-Dharma, and what is non-Dharma as Dharma; taking what is wrong to be right, he declared the Vinaya to be non-Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya to be Vinaya, coming to obstruct the *pravāraṇā*.
The Saṃgha should ask:
"Who among the assembly has committed an offense?
Furthermore, what is that offense?"
Is it a *pārājika*? Is it a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, or a *duṣkṛta*?
Is it during the day?
Is it night?
Is he traveling on the road?
Or is he by the side of the road?
Is it at the time of walking?
Is it at the time of standing?
Or is it at the time of sitting?
"Is it when one is lying down?
If he says: "One commits the four *pārājika* offenses, but does not commit the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or even the *duṣkṛta* offenses."
If one says: "I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, but I have not committed any of the four pārājika offenses, nor have I committed even a duṣkṛta offense. If one says:
"One commits a *pāyattika*, but does not commit a *pārājika* up to a *dukkaṭa*.
Or if one says:
"One commits a *praideśanīya*, but does not commit any of the four *pārājikas* up to a *dukkaṭa*."
If one says: "He has committed a *duṣkṛta*, but has not committed a *pārājika* up to a *prātideśanīya*.
Or if one says:
"If one commits the first *pārājika*, one does not commit the second, third, or even the fourth;
it is likewise for each. If one says:
"If one commits the second *pārājika*, one does not commit the first, nor the third, nor the fourth; it is likewise for each."
If one says: "I have committed the third *pārājika*, but have not committed the first, second, or fourth;
it is the same for the others. If one says:
"If one commits the first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one does not commit the second, nor even the thirteenth.
Or if one says:
"If one commits the second *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one does not commit the first, nor even the thirteenth."
If one says: "One commits the third *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, but does not commit the first, second, up to the eleventh," and so forth—
thus, for all thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*, the formulation of permutations through ascending and descending orders is to be understood as above.
If one says:
"I have committed the first *pāyattika*, but have not committed the second, nor even up to the ninetieth";
or if one says:
"This is the second, not the first or the third, up to the ninetieth.
In this manner, the formulation is applied in succession up to the ninetieth case in the same way.
If one says:
"I have committed a *pāṭidesanīya*, and this is the first [offense], not the second, nor even the fourth," the formulation is likewise for each case.
If one has committed the second [offense], and it is not the first, nor the third or fourth, the formulation of the sentence is likewise for each case.
If one says:
"I have committed a *duṣkṛta*, but this is the first offense, not the second," and so on up to the final [offense], it is likewise. If one says:
"This is an offense committed at night, not by day," some say; or they say,
"It is by day, not at night."
Some said: "This is the path;
that which is beside the path is not the path. Others said: "That which is beside the path is not the path;
this is the path. Or they said:
"The time of going is not the time of staying," or it is said:
"The time of staying is not the time of going."
Some said: "The time of standing is not the time of sitting. Others said:
"When sitting is not when standing," or as it is said:
"When sitting is not when reclining."
The rest is as above.
When this bhikṣu recounts these various matters, the assembly should question him thoroughly.
If what he says later contradicts what he said before, and thus his testimony is inconsistent, one should not accept his words.
If, after the Saṃgha has questioned him, his words do not differ [from what was previously reported], one should immediately ask:
"At the time you committed the offense, what were your physical gestures?
What words did you utter?"
With what intention did you act? If he says:
“I have committed a defeat.”
Those who say this should be expelled by the assembly before the *svacchanda* (formal declaration of purity) is performed. If they say:
"I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense," [the procedure continues accordingly].
Regarding this, one should first set aside that matter and perform the *svacchanda* (formal act of consent). If they say:
"I have committed a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or even a *dukkaṭa*," [one should proceed accordingly].
Regarding this, one should first express remorse before performing the *pravāraṇā*.
When the fifteenth day arrives and it is time for the *pravāraṇā*, many resident bhikṣus should assemble in one place; whether there be five or more, they shall perform the *pravāraṇā*.
Furthermore, there were some resident bhikṣus who did not come to join the assembly for the *pravāraṇā*.
Those bhikṣus then thought to themselves:
"There are bhikṣus here who have not come to this place; because of this, we have given rise to doubt."
"We did not wait for him to arrive; is this *pravāraṇā* now valid or invalid?
Having such doubts, they proceeded with the *pravāraṇā*.

When that junior bhikṣu later arrives at the assembly, he must perform the *pravāraṇā* again. Those who previously performed the *pravāraṇā* incur an offense against the Dharma (*dharmāpatti*) because it was performed improperly. The rest is as already explained in the section on the *poṣadha* rules.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, Great Virtuous One!

When a bhikṣu is observing the rains retreat and it is time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he asks himself: 'Are there no quarrelers, no revilers, no those who raise difficult questions, no those who intend to go to the houses of kings or officials, no those who have been imprisoned, and no those who have raised charges against others through illegitimate means who have come to this dwelling place? Are the bhikṣus currently residing here persons of integrity and modesty?'"
He asked again:
"When such quarrelsome and wicked people come, how should one act according to one's discretion?
The Buddha told Upāli:
"If such evil persons should come in haste, two or three people should go into the small boundary area (*kṣudrasīmā*) and perform the *svacchanda* (formal act of consent) among themselves.
If they succeed, it is well;
if they do not succeed, they should go out to meet them, take their robes and bowls for them, comfort and greet them, and speak to them with various gentle words."
Once one has entered the assigned dwelling, one should immediately perform the *kāyabandhana* (the ritual of assuming the informal posture).
If one obtains [the necessary requisites], it is well;
if one does not obtain them, one should perform the bathing ritual.
If they are willing to bathe, one person should be instructed to preach the Dharma while they listen; meanwhile, you yourself should quickly perform the *prātimokṣa* recitation (*poṣadha*).
If this is possible, it is well;
if not, you should personally go to a small boundary (*sīmā*) to perform the long purification.
If that bhikṣu should ask:
"Now is the time for the *pravāraṇā*; why do you perform the *poṣadha*? he should reply:
"You visiting bhikṣus, you must know that we, the long-term residents, have our own established rules.
The visiting bhikṣus said, "It is fitting;
let us perform the poṣadha together."
Once the matter was concluded and they had waited until the assembly had dispersed, they were to reconvene and perform the *pravāraṇā* separately.
If, while the *pravāraṇā* was being performed at a certain residence, a sick bhikṣu did not come from his room, how should the *pravāraṇā* be conducted?
One should reply to them:
"If you are able to come, then come.
If you are unable to come, you should bring what you intend to offer and come at your own convenience."
He sent a messenger to the sick bhikṣu, saying:
"Go to a place where you please.
It would be well if you were able to go.
If one is unable [to perform the *pravāraṇā*], one should grant consent (*chanda*) for the *pravāraṇā*.
At the time of the *pravāraṇā*, there are four possible situations:
there may be a matter but no person; there may be a person but no matter; there may be both; or there may be neither.
What is meant by "the presence of the matter but the absence of the person"?

It refers to when, during the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one lacks understanding and lacks discernment, being unskilled in recognizing what is beneficial and ignorant of how to perform what is wholesome.

If one stays near a dwelling place of a deity, or approaches such a dwelling, or [addresses] women or young girls, or utters various harsh words insulting that deity, or commits impure acts, or if the deity becomes angry and comes to the gate of the monastery, saying:
"O virtuous ones, what you have done is unwholesome and most improper; O virtuous ones, how could you possibly perform such and such deeds?"
Yet, one does not specifically state,
"So-and-so has committed an offense.
This is called "having the matter but no person."
What is meant by "there are people but no matter"?
When the time for the *yathāsukha* (distribution of robes) arrives, it is as explained extensively before.
A deity, having become enraged, came to the gate of the monastery and spoke these words:
"A certain bhikṣu has committed an offense against me," yet he does not say,
"There is such a fault or transgression."
This is called "having a person but no matter.
What is meant by "having both a matter and a person"?
It refers to stating both the offense and the name of the individual; this is called "having both a matter and a person."
What is meant by "neither person nor thing"?
Because both are non-existent, this is called the fourth [category].
